title: Truth, and truthful living
hookLine: truth is higher than everything, and higher still is truthful living (Sri Rag, ang 62)
tomorrow: Deeds as soil, the Word as seed

cards: Two people. One can win any argument about honesty: quote the rules, spot every white lie, explain exactly what truth is. Then watch how that one treats the waiter.

The other never talks about truth at all, but their word is solid, their yes means yes, and they return the extra change. Which of them has more truth in them? Guru Nanak answered in one line, on Ang 62.

teach.h: SACH, SAT — A NAME OF GOD.
teach.b: Sach means truth, and in the Guru Granth Sahib it's bigger than facts. Sach, or sat, is one of the names of God. Satnam, the True Name, comes right at the start of the Granth.

And Japji Sahib opens by saying, in paraphrase: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and, Nanak says, true forever. So truth isn't just something you tell. It's what's real, what lasts.
Now the twist. On Ang 62, in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak sings: sachahu orai sabh ko upar sach aachaar.
Everything is below truth; but higher still is truthful living. Aachaar means conduct, how you actually live. So there's something above even knowing the truth: living it.

The Gurus didn't separate belief and behavior. A person who speaks beautifully about God and cheats at work hasn't reached the top of the line. A farmer who never read a book, and whose dealings are straight, might have.
That's why the Sikh way leans so hard on the everyday: kirat karni, earning honestly; vand chhakna, sharing; the plain promise that your word is good.
Truth, for the Gurus, is something you can see in a person's hands and hear in their bargains. It's also why this is hard.
Knowing truth takes a clever mind. Living it takes every small moment of the day, including the ones nobody sees.

how: Sikhs quote Guru Nanak's line on truthful living (Ang 62) to describe the faith's emphasis on honest work, sharing and straight dealing in daily life, alongside remembering the Name.

o: a promise or vow made before witnesses
a hymn sung only at sunset
truth: what is real and lasts, a name of God

games.q: inside Guru Nanak's line — tap the pairs.

s: for Guru Nanak, knowing the truth is the highest thing
higher still, he says, is truthful living, sach aachaar.
in the Granth, sach is also a name of God
Satnam, the True Name, comes at the very start.
Japji Sahib opens by calling God true in the beginning, now and forever
true through the ages, true now, and true forever.

games.q: one person can explain truth perfectly but cheats at work. another never talks about it and deals straight. what does Guru Nanak's line put highest?
o: the one who explains truth best.
games.why: sachahu orai sabh ko upar sach aachaar: everything is below truth, and higher still is truthful living.

practice: Think of one small truth you'd usually skip, not a big confession, just a little one, like I haven't read it yet, or that was my mistake, or I'm not fine, actually, or I can't make it.
Picture saying it, simply and kindly, and notice what fear comes up, letting it be there. Then rest with the breath, steady and plain.

wordCard.voice: Sach. Truth, and in the Granth a name of God, what's real and lasts. And higher still than truth, Guru Nanak says, is truthful living.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sach, truth; in Gurbani it often carries a short final u sound in the spelling, sachu.

carryVoice: Your line: truth, lived. Knowing it is good; living it is higher. That's day two hundred forty-nine.
